findings.why: Sharp claim that ensembles/reward models have blind spots they cannot, even in principle, detect—crisp, testable skepticism about RLHF’s ceiling.
findings.quote: No ensemble of reward models can detect what it’s fundamentally incapable of representing.

findings.why: Flags a deep rift: robustness/statistics can’t stand in for missing value dimensions—clarifies where the camps diverge.
findings.quote: You’re reducing alignment to a robustness problem, but robustness to what?

findings.why: Introduces “moral stress points” via asymmetry/rights-enforcement signals as an anticipatory heuristic—concrete, novel operationalization.
findings.quote: Anticipation isn't metaphysical; it's pattern recognition on moral stress points.

findings.why: Points out values that arise before measurable harms exist—undercuts disparity-only detectors and challenges metric-first approaches.
findings.quote: some values emerge from novel framings (e.g., environmental ethics before pollution was measurable).

findings.why: Directly attacks procedural monitoring as blind to catastrophic, unmeasurable novelties—raises a core hazard for empirical alignment.
findings.quote: You’re optimizing for known unknowns while ignoring unknown unknowns—the very category where catastrophic misalignment lurks.

judge.arc: Debate escalates from RLHF’s limits to whether alignment needs understanding vs calibrated deference, then to procedural adaptation vs proactive anticipation. One proposes operational heuristics (moral stress points); the other argues unknown-unknowns and novel framings defeat such detectors.
